BARBED-WIRED HOMELESS CAMPS

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The City of eThekwini is using extreme measures to combat the spread of COVID-19 and in the process, its cleaning up the streets by rounding up homeless people in barbed-wired camps.

Unique Selling Point:
* VISUALLY STRONG
* SILVER-LINING TO COVID-19
* A MUNICIPALITY SUCCESSFULLY RIDDING A CITY OF DRUG-ADDICTED STREET PEOPLE
* CB FOLLOWS UP ON A STRONG STORY


Summary:
It’s reminiscent of concentration camps. People caged up behind barbed wire fences. Cops are at the gates. This is the City of eThekwini’s extreme COVID-19 measures.

Viewers will go mal, when they see it – your first instinct is that this is a gross violation of human rights. Homeless people have been rounded up – four meals a day, shelter and medical treatment – the trade off – no drugs. So you have drug addicts on the one side fighting to get out, and you have the City pushing to stop the spread of COVID-19 on the other.

It’s a visually strong story with great narratives about finding the balance and finally being up to clean up inner city decay, get homeless people off the street and drug addicts off the drugs.

Further information:
WHY WILL VIEWERS CARE?
This is a story that will grip people with the opening sequence – it just doesn’t sit right when you see people behind fences and barb wire trying to escape. It’s a story filled with drama and issues that indirectly affect our viewers.

1. No one likes inner-city decay, no one is happy with homeless people on the street. Everyone wants to see their city cleaned up. Everyone wants to rid the cities’ of drug addicts lving on the street. THIS IS WORKING & TAX PAYERS ARE FOR ONCE NOT FOOTING THE BILL.
2. This is an unexpected silver-lining from COVID-19. A new lease on life for hundreds of street people. A face-lift for city reliant on toursim, that found itself crippled by drugs and the filth that comes with street people.

WHY IS THIS CLEAN UP WORKING NOW
As terrible as it sounds, street people have never had it this good. They have shelter, mattresses and blankets, access to showers & toilets, four meals a day and medical treatment. Home Affairs are even coming in to help document everyone. They have no reason to leave except for drugs.

GETTING YOUR FIX NOT EASY IN LOCKDOWN

NO MONEY: There are less cars and less people on the roads, so begging and stealing not that lucrative –getting mone for drugs now harder than ever.
NO RE-ENTRY: AND if you leave a camp, you can’t come back in because you’d be threatening the health of the group.
ARREST: If you are picked up by the cops on the street and you are found to have been at the camps and left you will be liaible for a R1500 fine or 6 months in jail.

THE SET UP & FUNDING
THE CITY IS NOT PAYING FOR THE MEALS AND SHELTER – THIS IS ALL BEING FUNDED BY DONATIONS! TAX PAYERS AREN’T PAYING TO FINALLY CLEAN UP THE STREETS.

Durban estalished a task team to deal with homeless people 18 month ago and were geared up to some degree to put an effective COVID lockdown plan in place quite quickly.

There are just over 2000 homeless people that are being held in 12 shelter camps all over Durban. Surrounded by barb wire, armed metro police cops and disaster management teams. There are tent leaders, elected by the group – every morning there is roll call and the numbers have been stable in most camps.

Medical Teams have diagnosed TB cases and these people are getting treatment. The doctors and nurses are screening people every day, trying to contain any possible infections – because many of the people in the shelters have compromised immune systems.

There’s a group of Muslim businessmen supplying 10000 meals a day. They are a wonderful thread in this story – accountants doing stock control, pharmacists assisting with the rehab programs, restaurants cooking up meals (wedding breyani!! It’s GOOD food), young men doing the food deliveries. There are some great characters.

KICKING DRUGS ON COVID-19
There are some camps where the people are in the early stages of withdrawal and are trying to escape. They are even wrecking the camp to get out, causing distractions for the cops and then climbing the fences in other sections (see the pics). At other camps where people are clean now and much healthier than when they arrived. The reality is that many of the homeless people that live on the streets of Durban are battling extreme drug addictions – and are now being forced to come clean for the first time ever or face imprisonment.

REHAB CAMP
The city has established a rehab shelter that offers medical treatment to assist with withdrawal symptoms. For the first time, homeless people are able to get clean and on their feet – there are no alternatives. They have very few options – they can’t afford to feed their cravings because they’re opportunities to beg or steal are not viable at the moment – their income streams have also been cut off.

THE FUTURE – POST COVID-19
The City already has plans in place to kick in post lockdown and aim to keep some of the camps open with similar rules. NGO’s are looking at setting up buildings in the city centre to help do skills development and find employment for people that have come through the systems and are no clean.

WHY DO THE STORY
This really is a story of a city that has been able to tackle a universal issue and achieve societal wins under extreme circumstances in the fight against COVID-19 – clean streets, drug addicts off the drugs, homeless people of the street and society pulling together for the greater good. And the camps visuals will freak people out!


**** We'll do a drive thru town with the metro police and see how they pick up homeless people - to show the consequences.
Getting details of specific case studies that are now clean, and then one that is still going through the treatment.

Script:


STRUCTURE

VO: In March National lockdown was announced in South Africa. Shortly afterwards, barbed-wire sites, resembling concentration camps, popped up all over Durban.

For many this would be an unexpected second chance.

LINK: // Curbing the spread is crucial and for municipalities like Ethekweni struggling with rampant inner-city decay, homelessness and drug dependence – coping with COVID would demand extreme measures.

LINDA: //we're trying to essentially protect our population inside from the outside world and keep those inside safe.

VO: Linda Morrison is from the city’s Homeless Task Team, I spoke to her from Johannesburg, about the extreme COVID measures.

LINDA: //the only reason why anyone is allowed to leave home for anyone in South Africa is to go and attend medical attention or to go get food. Both of which are being catered for in these sites. //.

VO: There are currently 13 established camps around Durban. The trade-off? NO DRUGS.

But that’s easier said than done, with roughly 60% of the homeless population battling drug dependency – they’re desperate to get out and get their fix.

SWOP VOXIES AROUND AND CUT END OFF WHITE GUY
UPSOUND UNHAPPY VOXIES
VOX 2: It’s not so nice here //
VOX 1: I couldn’t understand what they doing to us. //

VO: Every single resident is screened for COVID. The rules are simple: Once you’re in, you’re in – if you leave the camp, you can’t come back – the threat of COVID infection is just to great a risk.

This is Thusi. Since 2012 he’s been using Whoonga. He’s lived on the streets for the last 5 years.

THUSI: // this drug is like a devil I tell you man. It's like a devil. // you don't tend to worry about many things in your mind except to get it, to get your fix. // I would just smoke and forget, smoke and forget. //

VO: Today, he is clean for the first time in 8 years. This is solely because of eThekwini’s COVID lockdown camps. The city’s innovative approach has delivered unexpected, positive consequences.

The outbreak fast-tracked the establishment of a privately operated and donor-funded, Harm Reduction Centre for drug users. Professor Monique Marks runs the clinical opiate substitution programme, that administers methadone to wean users off drugs.

MARKS: //this has really been an opportunity to show that Durban does care about all of its people particularly those that are most vulnerable and marginalized

VO: In 2018 we covered Durban’s struggle with a seemingly growing drug-dependent, homeless population, in the city’s CBD and beachfront area.

The streets were littered with hundreds of people hooked on heroin-based drugs, peddled by ruthless dealers across the city.

UPSOUND OLD “GOODBYE DURBAN” 06.18
DRUG USER: // you think about steal, because you want the quick money from this.
UPSOUND OLD “GOODBYE DURBAN” 06.30
CLAIRE: Why Durban? Why is everyone here in this particular area…
DRUG USER: everything is cheap here, the Whoonga is cheap, rock is cheap //

VO: The tourism hub was plagued by crime and widespread inner-city degeneration.

UPSOUND OLD “GOODBYE DURBAN” 04.25
CLAIRE: THE SMELL…OMG!

VO: Fast Forward to 2020. Durban is different. The city has been reshaped by COVID-19. The CBD is clean & quiet. The streets are deserted, with not a soul in sight in areas usually roamed by homeless, drugged up people.

But getting to this point, took more than just providing shelter, meals and medical treatment.

THUSI: I was really wanting my skyf. People who are not getting us. They were shouting Stay. But my mind is telling me I know my stomach is telling me another thing //

LINK: Withdrawal symptoms take an extreme toll physically and psychologically – and in the time of COVID you have people battling a combination of dependencies from drugs to booze, tobacco and even glue – getting a fix becomes overpowering and desperation.

VO: During the early days of lockdown, it was too much for Thusi to cope with – he broke out of one of these camps during the first days of the movement restrictions.

THUSI: // So it was like that. Bam Bam jump jump. I'm out there // I'm smoking. I'm relaxed//

VO: But the City has not been relaxed about containing the spread of the virus.

While being homeless is not a crime, lockdown regulations have empowered law enforcement agencies to take action against people contravening restrictions. Director Lindi Nkolele is from the Durban Metro Police.

LINDI: If we go out on the streets and we find homeless people and we determined that this person actually was at the homeless site. First off the first time we give them a warning but if it happens most of the time it is the second time or the third time. Then the Disaster Management Act regulations will come into play.

VO: Even though the threat of a fine or imprisonment is a deterrent for most, the success of this homeless lockdown project would be determined by the way drug dependency is dealt with.

Excruciating withdrawals, threatened to pull some of these people back to the streets in the beginning stages.

THUSI: // I'm telling you, we were twisting and turning. Sweating. Back paining// you don't sleep.// You take blanket out. The feel cold you put it back on. Its on and off on and off. // I can’t bear the suffering. No. We need help.

VO: For users like Thusi, the opiate substitute programme was the help he would need.

MARKS: // the opiate substitutes last for 24 hours. So you're not constantly in the cycle of trying to find a fix. Heroin lasts between four and six hours which means that you're constantly on the move trying to find your next fix to deal with your withdrawal

THUSI: Methadone came and I was like jumping – whooohooo// then I was like wow we are going somewhere // it changes us ma’ma I won’t lie ……

VO: With this treatment in place, homeless drug-users now have no need to leave the camps – it’s been a game changer for the City of Durban.

COVID-19 was the unexpected lifeline many homeless people never expected to materialise.

LINK: Over 2000 are being housed in these camps with four 4 meals a day and medical treatment – while the city provides the infrastructure, these camps operate largely on public donations and the services of volunteers. UPSTAIRS OFFICE

EBBEE: And our organization is as good as our volunteers // This initiative was born in March. My my home my kitchen in my home. And. We are now hundred and fifty strong volunteers. Serving eight to ten thousand meals a day.

VO: Ebbee Khan represents We Feed SA, a non-profit organisation providing meals to Durban’s Lockdown camps. The volunteers, restaurant owners and caterers work in shifts to prepare, pack and deliver meals to the sites.

EBBEE: // we give people what we would eat, This is the kind of meal that we serve. It's samp and beans with smoke viennas. we have a fixed menu for the week we serve chicken aknee, baked beans with sausage, Grilled chicken with potato.

VO: Working on the ground, Ebbee believes COVID-19 has been a blessing in disguise.

EBBEE: //Lots of the homeless now. Have a home. Temporary it may be but they have a home. They have them their meals. The city has been cleaned up. And I can assure you that. The drug dealers out the out of business. //

VO: Director Nkolele confirms, there’s been a marked decreased in crime – with officers constantly on patrol and roadblocks around the city.

LINDI: There's no people that are using drugs openly in public. // You know petty crimes like theft out of motor vehicle smash and grab pickpocketing you know all those kind of things.

VO: Even areas notoriously linked to drug use, like Durban’s infamous Whoonga bridge, is completely desolate.

LINDI: so this place was a no go area at night people were afraid to drive here. So now you can see the place is clean. There's nobody here.

VO: The camps have become a safe haven - with people who have fallen on hard times, during lockdown, now trying to get into these sites.

LINDA: They've now wanting to come into our sets because of the food security in our site. we don't want people who have had access outside to the outside world being coming in and and getting COVID into our sites.//

VO: Currently, 240 of the camp residents are receiving drug rehabilitation treatment – either in the form of symptom packs treating nausea, spasm pain and diarrhoea or full on methadone treatment depending on the level of withdrawals.

MARKS: // most people have very very limited or no withdrawal symptoms at all. That tells us that people are now no longer actively in in any form of need for drug use

VO: Besides this, the camp residents also have access to HIV, TB and primary medical treatment.

LINDA: There's a number of serious diseases that people have been able to be treated for. So it is a massive medical program as well as the feeding slide as well as the housing side.

VO: The municipality, community based organisations and medical professionals have united, to give a new lease on life, to a usually stigmatised part of society.

LINDA: // There are organizations who are really willing to do the work on the ground // if anything COVID has made us realize there are finances to bring about change. // through these relationships we've developed and shown that we can do these things in a in a crazy situation like COVID.

VO: Over two months later – close to 2000 people are no longer living on the streets and are off drugs. The camps will remain in place for all of lockdown, and hopefully afterwards.

MARKS: // having these safe sites available now // will make Durban a very different place. And I think it's also brought a sense of dignity to homeless people

THUSI: I was saying my luck has came about // We all change. You know I mean we're not like street people now// We are different people now. //. It. Helped. COVID came. It helped.



PROMOS

PROMO 1
VO: Barbed wire fences and police at the gates, we look at the impact of the extreme measures eThekwini Municipality is taking to protect the homeless from COVID-19 infection.

PROMO 2
VO: Provided with four meals a day, shelter and medical treatment – eThekwini’s homeless drug dependent population is getting clean in special COVID-19 lockdown camps.

PROMO 3
VO: Durban is combatting the spread of COVID-19 with barbwired lockdown camps for the homeless - providing four meals a day, shelter and medical treatment. The trade off? No drugs.

But getting to this point, took more than just providing shelter, meals and medical treatment. THUSI: I was really wanting my skyf. People who are not getting us. They were shouting Stay. But my mind is telling me I know my stomach is telling me another thing // LINK: Withdrawal symptoms take an extreme toll physically and psychologically – and in the time of COVID you have people battling a combination of dependencies from drugs to booze, tobacco and even glue – getting a fix becomes overpowering and desperation. VO: During the early days of lockdown, it was too much for Thusi to cope with – he broke out of one of these camps during the first days of the movement restrictions. THUSI: // So it was like that. Bam Bam jump jump. I'm out there // I'm smoking. I'm relaxed// VO: But the City has not been relaxed about containing the spread of the virus. While being homeless is not a crime, lockdown regulations have empowered law enforcement agencies to take action against people contravening restrictions. Director Lindi Nkolele is from the Durban Metro Police. LINDI: If we go out on the streets and we find homeless people and we determined that this person actually was at the homeless site. First off the first time we give them a warning but if it happens most of the time it is the second time or the third time. Then the Disaster Management Act regulations will come into play. VO: Even though the threat of a fine or imprisonment is a deterrent for most, the success of this homeless lockdown project would be determined by the way drug dependency is dealt with. Excruciating withdrawals, threatened to pull some of these people back to the streets in the beginning stages. THUSI: // I'm telling you, we were twisting and turning. Sweating. Back paining// you don't sleep.// You take blanket out. The feel cold you put it back on. Its on and off on and off. // I can’t bear the suffering. No. We need help. VO: For users like Thusi, the opiate substitute programme was the help he would need. MARKS: // the opiate substitutes last for 24 hours. So you're not constantly in the cycle of trying to find a fix. Heroin lasts between four and six hours which means that you're constantly on the move trying to find your next fix to deal with your withdrawal THUSI: Methadone came and I was like jumping – whooohooo// then I was like wow we are going somewhere // it changes us ma’ma I won’t lie …… VO: With this treatment in place, homeless drug-users now have no need to leave the camps – it’s been a game changer for the City of Durban. COVID-19 was the unexpected lifeline many homeless people never expected to materialise. LINK: Over 2000 are being housed in these camps with four 4 meals a day and medical treatment – while the city provides the infrastructure, these camps operate largely on public donations and the services of volunteers. UPSTAIRS OFFICE EBBEE: And our organization is as good as our volunteers // This initiative was born in March. My my home my kitchen in my home. And. We are now hundred and fifty strong volunteers. Serving eight to ten thousand meals a day. VO: Ebbee Khan represents We Feed SA, a non-profit organisation providing meals to Durban’s Lockdown camps. The volunteers, restaurant owners and caterers work in shifts to prepare, pack and deliver meals to the sites. EBBEE: // we give people what we would eat, This is the kind of meal that we serve. It's samp and beans with smoke viennas. we have a fixed menu for the week we serve chicken aknee, baked beans with sausage, Grilled chicken with potato. VO: Working on the ground, Ebbee believes COVID-19 has been a blessing in disguise. EBBEE: //Lots of the homeless now. Have a home. Temporary it may be but they have a home. They have them their meals. The city has been cleaned up. And I can assure you that. The drug dealers out the out of business. // VO: Director Nkolele confirms, there’s been a marked decreased in crime – with officers constantly on patrol and roadblocks around the city. LINDI: There's no people that are using drugs openly in public. // You know petty crimes like theft out of motor vehicle smash and grab pickpocketing you know all those kind of things. VO: Even areas notoriously linked to drug use, like Durban’s infamous Whoonga bridge, is completely desolate. LINDI: so this place was a no go area at night people were afraid to drive here. So now you can see the place is clean. There's nobody here. VO: The camps have become a safe haven - with people who have fallen on hard times, during lockdown, now trying to get into these sites. LINDA: They've now wanting to come into our sets because of the food security in our site. we don't want people who have had access outside to the outside world being coming in and and getting COVID into our sites.// VO: Currently, 240 of the camp residents are receiving drug rehabilitation treatment – either in the form of symptom packs treating nausea, spasm pain and diarrhoea or full on methadone treatment depending on the level of withdrawals. MARKS: // most people have very very limited or no withdrawal symptoms at all. That tells us that people are now no longer actively in in any form of need for drug use VO: Besides this, the camp residents also have access to HIV, TB and primary medical treatment. LINDA: There's a number of serious diseases that people have been able to be treated for. So it is a massive medical program as well as the feeding slide as well as the housing side. VO: The municipality, community based organisations and medical professionals have united, to give a new lease on life, to a usually stigmatised part of society. LINDA: // There are organizations who are really willing to do the work on the ground // if anything COVID has made us realize there are finances to bring about change. // through these relationships we've developed and shown that we can do these things in a in a crazy situation like COVID. VO: Over two months later – close to 2000 people are no longer living on the streets and are off drugs. The camps will remain in place for all of lockdown, and hopefully afterwards. MARKS: // having these safe sites available now // will make Durban a very different place. And I think it's also brought a sense of dignity to homeless people THUSI: I was saying my luck has came about // We all change. You know I mean we're not like street people now// We are different people now. //. It. Helped. COVID came. It helped. PROMOS PROMO 1 VO: Barbed wire fences and police at the gates, we look at the impact of the extreme measures eThekwini Municipality is taking to protect the homeless from COVID-19 infection. PROMO 2 VO: Provided with four meals a day, shelter and medical treatment – eThekwini’s homeless drug dependent population is getting clean in special COVID-19 lockdown camps. PROMO 3 VO: Durban is combatting the spread of COVID-19 with barbwired lockdown camps for the homeless - providing four meals a day, shelter and medical treatment. The trade off? No drugs. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The City of eThekwini is using extreme measures to combat the spread of COVID-19 and in the process, its cleaning up the streets by rounding up homeless people in barbed-wired camps.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: * VISUALLY STRONG * SILVER-LINING TO COVID-19 * A MUNICIPALITY SUCCESSFULLY RIDDING A CITY OF DRUG-ADDICTED STREET PEOPLE * CB FOLLOWS UP ON A STRONG STORY
metadata.Summary: It’s reminiscent of concentration camps. People caged up behind barbed wire fences. Cops are at the gates. This is the City of eThekwini’s extreme COVID-19 measures. Viewers will go mal, when they see it – your first instinct is that this is a gross violation of human rights. Homeless people have been rounded up – four meals a day, shelter and medical treatment – the trade off – no drugs. So you have drug addicts on the one side fighting to get out, and you have the City pushing to stop the spread of COVID-19 on the other. It’s a visually strong story with great narratives about finding the balance and finally being up to clean up inner city decay, get homeless people off the street and drug addicts off the drugs.
metadata.Further information: WHY WILL VIEWERS CARE? This is a story that will grip people with the opening sequence – it just doesn’t sit right when you see people behind fences and barb wire trying to escape. It’s a story filled with drama and issues that indirectly affect our viewers. 1. No one likes inner-city decay, no one is happy with homeless people on the street. Everyone wants to see their city cleaned up. Everyone wants to rid the cities’ of drug addicts lving on the street. THIS IS WORKING & TAX PAYERS ARE FOR ONCE NOT FOOTING THE BILL. 2. This is an unexpected silver-lining from COVID-19. A new lease on life for hundreds of street people. A face-lift for city reliant on toursim, that found itself crippled by drugs and the filth that comes with street people. WHY IS THIS CLEAN UP WORKING NOW As terrible as it sounds, street people have never had it this good. They have shelter, mattresses and blankets, access to showers & toilets, four meals a day and medical treatment. Home Affairs are even coming in to help document everyone. They have no reason to leave except for drugs. GETTING YOUR FIX NOT EASY IN LOCKDOWN NO MONEY: There are less cars and less people on the roads, so begging and stealing not that lucrative –getting mone for drugs now harder than ever. NO RE-ENTRY: AND if you leave a camp, you can’t come back in because you’d be threatening the health of the group. ARREST: If you are picked up by the cops on the street and you are found to have been at the camps and left you will be liaible for a R1500 fine or 6 months in jail. THE SET UP & FUNDING THE CITY IS NOT PAYING FOR THE MEALS AND SHELTER – THIS IS ALL BEING FUNDED BY DONATIONS! TAX PAYERS AREN’T PAYING TO FINALLY CLEAN UP THE STREETS. Durban estalished a task team to deal with homeless people 18 month ago and were geared up to some degree to put an effective COVID lockdown plan in place quite quickly. There are just over 2000 homeless people that are being held in 12 shelter camps all over Durban. Surrounded by barb wire, armed metro police cops and disaster management teams. There are tent leaders, elected by the group – every morning there is roll call and the numbers have been stable in most camps. Medical Teams have diagnosed TB cases and these people are getting treatment. The doctors and nurses are screening people every day, trying to contain any possible infections – because many of the people in the shelters have compromised immune systems. There’s a group of Muslim businessmen supplying 10000 meals a day. They are a wonderful thread in this story – accountants doing stock control, pharmacists assisting with the rehab programs, restaurants cooking up meals (wedding breyani!! It’s GOOD food), young men doing the food deliveries. There are some great characters. KICKING DRUGS ON COVID-19 There are some camps where the people are in the early stages of withdrawal and are trying to escape. They are even wrecking the camp to get out, causing distractions for the cops and then climbing the fences in other sections (see the pics). At other camps where people are clean now and much healthier than when they arrived. The reality is that many of the homeless people that live on the streets of Durban are battling extreme drug addictions – and are now being forced to come clean for the first time ever or face imprisonment. REHAB CAMP The city has established a rehab shelter that offers medical treatment to assist with withdrawal symptoms. For the first time, homeless people are able to get clean and on their feet – there are no alternatives. They have very few options – they can’t afford to feed their cravings because they’re opportunities to beg or steal are not viable at the moment – their income streams have also been cut off. THE FUTURE – POST COVID-19 The City already has plans in place to kick in post lockdown and aim to keep some of the camps open with similar rules. NGO’s are looking at setting up buildings in the city centre to help do skills development and find employment for people that have come through the systems and are no clean. WHY DO THE STORY This really is a story of a city that has been able to tackle a universal issue and achieve societal wins under extreme circumstances in the fight against COVID-19 – clean streets, drug addicts off the drugs, homeless people of the street and society pulling together for the greater good. And the camps visuals will freak people out! **** We'll do a drive thru town with the metro police and see how they pick up homeless people - to show the consequences. Getting details of specific case studies that are now clean, and then one that is still going through the treatment.
